They give A′B′/AB = −v/−u = (−v + f)/−f, using the sign convention.

text: Derive the lens maker’s formula for a thin lens of refractive index n in air.

points.text: Refraction at the first surface gives n/v₁ − 1/u = (n − 1)/R₁.
Refraction at the second surface gives 1/v − n/v₁ = (1 − n)/R₂.
Adding them removes v₁, which gives 1/v − 1/u = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂).
For an object at infinity, v = f, so 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂).
Conclusion: focal length depends on the index and the two radii.

Since r₁ + r₂ = A, we get r = A/2.
Since i + e = A + δ and i = e, we get i = (A + δₘ)/2.
Substituting into Snell’s law gives the result.

facts: p12-6a:the principal axis of a mirror
p12-6a:the centre of curvature of a spherical mirror
p12-6a:the pole of a spherical mirror
p12-6a:dispersion
text:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A
(1) the principal axis of a mirror
(2) the centre of curvature of a spherical mirror
(3) the pole of a spherical mirror
(4) dispersion
Column B
(a) The splitting of white light into its colours, because the refractive index differs from colour to colour.
(b) The line through its pole and its centre of curvature.
(c) The centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part.
(d) The centre of its reflecting surface.

points.text: (1) the principal axis of a mirror goes with (b).
(2) the centre of curvature of a spherical mirror goes with (c).
(3) the pole of a spherical mirror goes with (d).
(4) dispersion goes with (a).

p12-6a:the critical angle
text:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A
(1) angle of minimum deviation
(2) power of a lens
(3) the principal focus of a convex lens
(4) the critical angle
Column B
(a) The smallest angle through which a prism turns a ray, occurring when the ray passes through it symmetrically.
(b) The point on the axis where rays parallel to the axis meet after passing through the lens.
(c) The reciprocal of its focal length in metres.
(d) The angle of incidence in a denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°.

points.text: (1) angle of minimum deviation goes with (a).
(2) power of a lens goes with (c).
(3) the principal focus of a convex lens goes with (b).
(4) the critical angle goes with (d).

text: A photographer tests a camera lens. Situation: Magnification (lens). The image distance is doubled and the object distance is made four times as large. By what factor does the magnification change?
why: The magnification varies in direct proportion to the image distance, and the magnification varies in inverse proportion to the object distance, so the factor is $2^{1} \times 4^{-1}$ = 0.5. The other options come from common slips: 8 if you ignored the powers in the relation; 2 if you turned the ratio upside down; 0.25 if you changed only the object distance.

why: The magnifying power varies in direct proportion to the objective focal length, and the magnifying power varies in inverse proportion to the eyepiece focal length, so the factor is $2^{1} \times 4^{-1}$ = 0.5. The other options come from common slips: 8 if you ignored the powers in the relation; 2 if you turned the ratio upside down; 0.25 if you changed only the eyepiece focal length.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:a wavefront
text: Define a wavefront.

points.text: The surface through points of a wave that are all in the same phase.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:coherent sources
text: Define coherent sources.

points.text: Sources of the same frequency with a constant phase difference.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:coherent sources
text: State what is meant by coherent sources, and add one further point about it.

points.text: Sources of the same frequency with a constant phase difference.
In practice they are made from one source, as by the two slits in Young’s experiment.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Huygens’ principle
text: Define Huygens’ principle.

points.text: Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets, and the new wavefront is the common tangent to them after a given time.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:a spherical wavefront
text: Define a spherical wavefront.

points.text: The wavefront spreading out from a point source.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:a plane wavefront
text: Define a plane wavefront.

points.text: A wavefront from a very distant source, in which the rays are parallel.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:a cylindrical wavefront
text: Define a cylindrical wavefront.

points.text: The wavefront from a line source, such as a slit.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:interference of light
text: Define interference of light.

points.text: The change in intensity when two coherent light waves overlap, giving bright and dark fringes.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:constructive interference
text: Define constructive interference.

points.text: Waves meeting in phase, so that they add to give a greater amplitude.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:destructive interference
text: Define destructive interference.

points.text: Waves meeting out of phase by half a cycle, so that they partly or wholly cancel.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:fringe width
text: Define fringe width.

points.text: The distance between two consecutive bright fringes or two consecutive dark fringes.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:fringe width
text: State what is meant by fringe width, and add one further point about it.

points.text: The distance between two consecutive bright fringes or two consecutive dark fringes.
In Young’s experiment, it equals λD/d.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:path difference
text: Define path difference.

points.text: The difference in the distances travelled by two waves to reach a point.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:phase difference
text: Define phase difference.

points.text: The difference in phase between two waves at a point, equal to 2π/λ times the path difference.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:sustained interference
text: Define sustained interference.

points.text: An interference pattern that stays fixed in position for as long as it is observed.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:diffraction of light
text: Define diffraction of light.

points.text: The bending of light around an edge or through a narrow opening, into the region of geometrical shadow.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Fraunhofer diffraction
text: Define Fraunhofer diffraction.

points.text: Diffraction in which the source and screen are effectively at infinity, so the wavefronts are plane.

facts: p12-6c:Two separate lamps don’t give steady interference fringes.
text: Give a reason: Two separate lamps don’t give steady interference fringes.

points.text: They aren’t coherent, as their phase difference keeps changing.
So the pattern shifts too fast to see.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Diffraction of sound is easily noticed, but that of light isn’t.
text: Give a reason: Diffraction of sound is easily noticed, but that of light isn’t.

points.text: Sound has wavelengths comparable with everyday openings.
Light has a far smaller wavelength.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Young’s fringes can’t be seen if the slits are very wide.
text: Give a reason: Young’s fringes can’t be seen if the slits are very wide.

points.text: Each wide slit gives its own spread of fringes, shifted from the others.
These overlap, so the pattern blurs into even light.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Two separate sodium lamps give no fringes.
text: Give a reason: Two separate sodium lamps give no fringes.

points.text: Each atom emits at random, so their phase difference changes very quickly.
The pattern shifts too fast to be seen.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Fringes vanish if one of the slits in Young’s experiment is covered.
text: Give a reason: Fringes vanish if one of the slits in Young’s experiment is covered.

points.text: Only one wave now reaches the screen, so there is nothing to interfere with it.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Fringes would be too close to see if the slits were much farther apart.
text: Give a reason: Fringes would be too close to see if the slits were much farther apart.

points.text: Fringe width is inversely proportional to the slit separation.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Monochromatic light is preferred in Young’s experiment.
text: Give a reason: Monochromatic light is preferred in Young’s experiment.

points.text: Each colour has its own fringe width, so several colours make the fringes overlap and blur.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Light doesn’t appear to bend around everyday objects.
text: Give a reason: Light doesn’t appear to bend around everyday objects.

points.text: Its wavelength is very small compared with the sizes of those objects.

facts: p12-6c:interference | diffraction
text: Distinguish between interference and diffraction.

points.text: Interference: Superposition of waves from two coherent sources. Diffraction: Superposition of wavelets from one wavefront.
Interference: Bright fringes are about equally bright. Diffraction: Brightness of the maxima falls away from the centre.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:interference | diffraction

points.text: Interference: Superposition of waves from two coherent sources. Diffraction: Superposition of wavelets from one wavefront.
Interference: Bright fringes are about equally bright. Diffraction: Brightness of the maxima falls away from the centre.
Interference: Fringe widths are about equal. Diffraction: The central maximum is twice as wide as the others.

facts: p12-6c:Fringe width is directly proportional to wavelength.
text: Which one of the following statements is true?

options.text: For sustained interference, the sources should be very far apart.
With white light in Young’s experiment, all the fringes are pure white.
Fringe width is directly proportional to wavelength.
Only the centre of a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets.

why: Fringe width is directly proportional to wavelength.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Fringe width is directly proportional to wavelength.
text: Which one of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets.
For sustained interference, the sources should be close together.
With white light in Young’s experiment, the fringes close to the centre are coloured with red outside.
Fringe width is inversely proportional to wavelength.

why: This one is false. In fact: Fringe width is directly proportional to wavelength.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Fringe width is directly proportional to wavelength.
text: A student writes: “Fringe width is inversely proportional to wavelength.” Say what is wrong with this, and write the statement correctly.

points.text: Fringe width is directly proportional to wavelength.

facts: p12-6c:Interference redistributes energy, but conserves it overall.
text: Which one of the following statements is true?

options.text: Immersing a double slit in water widens the fringes.
Huygens’ construction gives n₁ sin r = n₂ sin i for refraction.
Interference redistributes energy, but conserves it overall.
A wavefront is a surface of points in different phases.

why: Interference redistributes energy, but conserves it overall.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Interference redistributes energy, but conserves it overall.
text: Which one of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: Immersing a double slit in water narrows the fringes.
Huygens’ construction gives n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r for refraction.
Interference destroys energy at dark fringes.
A wavefront is a surface of points in the same phase.

why: This one is false. In fact: Interference redistributes energy, but conserves it overall.

subject: physics
facts: p12-6c:Interference redistributes energy, but conserves it overall.
text: A student writes: “Interference destroys energy at dark fringes.” Say what is wrong with this, and write the statement correctly.

options.text: Coherent sources have a phase difference that changes randomly.

facts: p12-6c:Immersing a double slit in water narrows the fringes.

options.text: Coherent sources have a constant phase difference.
In interference, all the bright fringes have about the same width and intensity.
A larger slit separation in Young’s experiment gives narrower fringes.
Immersing a double slit in water widens the fringes.

Column A

The other options come from common slips: 0.5 if you ignored the powers in the relation; 0.125 if you turned the ratio upside down; 2 if you changed only the wavelength.

why: The fringe width is 0.00105 m. The others keep too many figures, or have the wrong power of ten.

subject: physics
text: A gemstone’s sparkle is studied by a jeweller. Situation: Wavelength and frequency in a medium. The refractive index is halved and the wavelength in vacuum is tripled. By what factor does the wavelength in the medium change?
why: The wavelength in the medium varies in inverse proportion to the refractive index, and the wavelength in the medium varies in direct proportion to the wavelength in vacuum, so the factor is $0.5^{-1} \times 3^{1}$ = 6. The other options come from common slips: 1.5 if you ignored the powers in the relation; 0.167 if you turned the ratio upside down; 2 if you changed only the refractive index.
